@graph.headline: Option Trading Strategies: The Complete Guide
@graph.description: Option strategies by market view: straddle, strangle, iron condor, butterfly, covered call, protective put — breakeven, max profit, max loss, when each fails.

acceptedAnswer.text: Option trading strategies are combinations of option legs — bought and sold calls and puts, sometimes alongside shares you own — chosen to create a defined risk-reward profile for a particular market view. Instead of betting only on direction, a strategy can bet on a big move in either direction, on a range holding, on income from a holding, or on protection for a holding. The legs, not any single option, create the payoff.

mainEntity.name: Which option trading strategy is best for beginners?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single best strategy for beginners — fit depends on your market view, as the chooser table above shows. Sensible starting points are defined-risk structures with a small size: a covered call or protective put around shares you already own, or a long straddle or strangle around a known event where the total premium paid is the known maximum loss. Naked selling is excluded for beginners entirely, because its risk is undefined. Start small, paper-trade first, and size from the maximum loss.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a straddle and a strangle?

acceptedAnswer.text: A straddle buys a call and a put at the same strike; a strangle buys an out-of-the-money call and an out-of-the-money put at different strikes. The straddle costs more — ₹350 per share in this guide's illustration against ₹185 for the strangle — but needs a smaller move to profit, with breakevens of ₹24,650 and ₹25,350 against the strangle's ₹24,315 and ₹25,685. The strangle is cheaper; the straddle is more likely to profit. Both lose to time decay in flat markets and to volatility collapse after an event.

An iron condor sells an out-of-the-money put spread and an out-of-the-money call spread with the same expiry, for a net credit. It profits when the underlying stays between the two short strikes. Maximum profit is the net credit received (₹120 per share in this guide's illustration); maximum loss is the spread width minus the credit (₹500 − ₹120 = ₹380). The long legs hedge the short legs, which is what makes the risk defined — and the loss-to-profit ratio is why sizing matters more than win rate.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between an iron condor and a butterfly spread?

acceptedAnswer.text: A condor profits across a range; a butterfly profits at a point. The iron condor in this guide profits anywhere between its short strikes (₹24,380 to ₹25,620 after the credit), while the butterfly profits only between ₹24,585 and ₹25,415, peaking at the middle strike of ₹25,000. The condor's winning zone is wider but its maximum profit is smaller (₹120 against the butterfly's ₹415 in these illustrations); the butterfly's maximum profit is larger but its zone is far narrower. Wider zone, smaller prize versus narrower zone, bigger prize — that is the trade-off.

A covered call means owning the underlying and selling a call against it. You collect the premium (₹35 per share in this guide's illustration, selling the 1,900 call against shares bought at ₹1,850), which lowers your breakeven to ₹1,815 and caps your maximum profit at ₹85 per share. The premium cushions small falls but does not prevent large ones, and in a strong rally you give up all gains above the strike. It is an income-for-upside trade, not downside protection.

A protective put means owning the underlying and buying a put against it. In this guide's illustration you hold shares bought at ₹1,850 and buy the 1,750 put for ₹28, which caps your maximum loss at ₹128 per share while keeping unlimited upside minus the premium. The breakeven rises to ₹1,878. The cost is recurring: in flat markets the premium drags returns, month after month, which is the price of the floor.

mainEntity.name: How do you choose an option strategy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Choose in this order: market view first, then volatility view, then defined versus undefined risk, then affordability in lots. A big unknown-direction move points to a straddle or strangle; a range points to an iron condor or butterfly; a holding you want income from points to a covered call; a holding you want protected points to a protective put. Then size from the maximum loss, write down your exit before entry, and pick the failure mode you can live with — because every strategy fails in its own specific way, and that failure, not the best-case payoff, is what you are really choosing.
